questions.stem: On a hot, dry, windy day, a plant wilts more quickly than on a cool, humid, still day. Which factor has the greatest overall effect on increasing transpiration rate?

options.text: Temperature alone
Wind speed alone
The combination of all three factors: heat increases evaporation, low humidity maintains the diffusion gradient, and wind removes humid air from around leaves
Soil moisture level

questions.explanation: All three factors work together to increase transpiration. Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, speeding evaporation. Low humidity maintains a steep diffusion gradient (high water vapour inside the leaf, low outside). Wind removes the layer of humid air around the leaf, maintaining the diffusion gradient. Together, they cause maximum water loss.

questions.stem: A student measures transpiration rate in four conditions. Which condition would produce the LOWEST transpiration rate?

options.text: High temperature, low humidity, high wind speed
Low temperature, high humidity, low wind speed
High temperature, high humidity, high wind speed
Low temperature, low humidity, high wind speed

questions.explanation: Low temperature reduces evaporation rate from mesophyll cells. High humidity means the air outside the leaf already contains lots of water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient driving diffusion. Low wind speed means humid air accumulates around the leaf, further reducing the gradient. All three conditions minimise transpiration.

questions.stem: Light intensity is also a factor affecting transpiration, even though light itself does not cause evaporation. How does light indirectly increase transpiration?

options.text: Light heats the water in xylem vessels
Light causes stomata to open for gas exchange (CO2 for photosynthesis), which also allows water vapour to escape
Light breaks down water molecules in the leaf
Light increases the humidity inside the leaf

questions.explanation: In light, stomata open to allow CO2 in for photosynthesis. However, open stomata also allow water vapour to escape. In darkness, stomata close (no need for CO2), which reduces water loss. This is why transpiration rate is much higher during the day than at night. It represents a trade-off between gas exchange and water conservation.

questions.stem: A greenhouse grower mists their plants with water on hot days. How does this reduce wilting?

options.text: The water is absorbed directly through the leaves
Misting increases humidity around the leaves, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient and slowing transpiration
The water cools the soil, helping roots absorb more water
Misting blocks the stomata, preventing all gas exchange

questions.explanation: Misting increases the humidity of the air surrounding the leaves. This reduces the concentration gradient of water vapour between the inside of the leaf (saturated) and the surrounding air. With a smaller gradient, water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly, reducing the rate of transpiration and helping prevent wilting.

questions.stem: A plant with a large number of stomata on its leaves would be expected to have a higher transpiration rate than one with fewer stomata. However, a student finds that a desert cactus has very few stomata. How does this relate to its environment?

options.text: The cactus does not need to photosynthesise
Having fewer stomata reduces water loss through transpiration, which is essential for survival in a dry desert environment
Cacti absorb water through their spines instead
Desert air is too humid for transpiration

questions.explanation: In deserts, water is extremely scarce. Cacti have evolved to minimise water loss by having very few stomata (and often opening them only at night when it is cooler). Their leaves are reduced to spines (reducing surface area), and their thick, waxy stems store water. These are adaptations that prioritise water conservation over maximum photosynthetic rate.
